summary: Congestion Exposure lets senders tell the network about expected congestion, based on feedback about earlier packets in the flow. This experimental RFC describes the changes TCP needs in order to use ConEx.

eli5.summary: A driver tells the road crew how many traffic jams they expect. This explains how TCP can give that heads-up.

questions: what is congestion exposure in tcp
how does conex signal packet loss
subtitle: Senders signal expected congestion to the network for better traffic management

tldr.problem: Networks have limited visibility into which TCP flows cause congestion, making it hard to manage traffic fairly and prevent congestion collapse without affecting well-behaved flows.
tldr.mechanism: ConEx TCP senders track packet loss and ECN marks from congestion feedback, then mark outgoing packets with ConEx flags to inform network nodes how much congestion the flow has caused and will cause, enabling congestion-aware traffic management.
tldr.outcome: Network nodes can audit ConEx-marked traffic and apply congestion management (rate limiting, priority changes) proportionally to flows that actually cause congestion, rather than blindly managing flows by volume.

facts.label: Minimum credit in Slow Start
facts.value: Half of bytes in flight per RTT

today: RFC 7786 remains Experimental. No major ISPs have deployed ConEx audit functions at scale. The RFC invites further experimentation with audit algorithms, credit settings, and interactions with existing AQM and traffic management. More work is also needed on accurate ECN feedback to improve ConEx signal precision.

sections.title: Congestion Accountability
sections.content:
TCP's congestion control has worked well to prevent network collapse, but it treats all flows equally. A sender that backs off responsibly after experiencing loss is indistinguishable from an aggressive sender that ignores congestion feedback. Network operators need better visibility into which flows actually cause congestion to apply traffic management and pricing fairly.

Congestion Exposure (ConEx) allows TCP senders to signal their congestion responsibility directly to the network. When a sender experiences loss or ECN (Explicit Congestion Notification) marks, it not only backs off (as TCP normally does) but also marks its packets to inform network auditing functions about the congestion it caused. This enables flow-based congestion management—treating flows proportionally to their actual network impact rather than blindly.
sections.eli5: ConEx is like a speeding ticket for data. If your packets cause congestion, you have to admit it. The network can then charge you or slow you down fairly based on how much congestion you actually caused.

sections.title: Tracking Congestion with Two Counters
sections.content:
A ConEx TCP sender maintains two independent counters. The Loss Exposure Gauge (LEG) accumulates bytes that were lost due to congestion; when the sender detects a loss, it increases LEG by the payload size. The sender then marks subsequent packets with the L flag, reducing LEG by the packet size each time, until LEG reaches zero. This way, the sender eventually marks as many bytes as were lost.

The Congestion Exposure Gauge (CEG) works similarly for ECN-marked packets. When the sender receives an ACK indicating ECN marks were received, it increases CEG by an estimate of the marked bytes and then marks outgoing packets with the E flag to signal this. Both counters can go negative, indicating the sender has over-marked (a conservative but necessary approach given the uncertainty of packet loss).
sections.eli5: The sender keeps two tally sheets: one counting lost bytes and one counting ECN-marked bytes. As the sender ships packets, it marks them to 'pay off' what it owes the network.

sections.title: ConEx Flag Marking
sections.content:
All TCP packets carrying payload MUST be marked with the X (ConEx-capable) flag. When LEG or CEG is positive, the sender marks packets with the L or E flag respectively. The sender also signals credit by marking packets with the C flag to pre-announce that it may cause future congestion. The Credit State Counter (CSC) tracks credit availability. A conservative approach maintains credits equal to the bytes in flight, assuming all packets could be lost. During TCP Slow Start, the minimum credit is half the bytes in flight per RTT to match the exponential growth of congestion window size.

ConEx can operate in several modes depending on receiver capabilities: with SACK and accurate ECN (most accurate), with just SACK, with just ECN, or with neither. The RFC details algorithms for each mode, though SACK and ECN together provide the most accurate congestion accounting.
sections.eli5: Every packet gets marked with an X to say it is ConEx-aware. Packets carry L and E flags to repay past congestion, and C flags to warn that more congestion is coming. The network auditor checks: 'Did this flow mark itself for all the congestion it caused?'

sections.title: Deployment Considerations
sections.content:
ConEx requires changes only to TCP senders; receivers need no modification. However, effective ConEx depends on the entire path having audit functions that can observe and police ConEx flags. Without audits, ConEx signals are simply ignored. The RFC calls this an area for further experimentation—auditing algorithms, policies for how to penalize insufficient ConEx signals, and how to integrate audits with existing AQM (Active Queue Management) and traffic shaping.

A practical risk is that ConEx packets themselves can be lost, doubling the congestion signal paradoxically. The RFC notes this is a second-order problem due to low loss rates but recommends senders retransmit ConEx signals if ConEx-marked packets are lost.
sections.eli5: ConEx marks are only useful if the network is listening. The network needs audit functions to check ConEx marks and enforce fairness. Without them, ConEx becomes a voluntary honor system.

sections.title: Timing and Accuracy
sections.content:
ConEx signals are only useful to the network within about one RTT of the congestion event. If congestion happened an RTT ago, marking packets now is too late to prevent that particular congestion. Therefore, senders must mark packets as soon as congestion feedback arrives. This creates tension with the TCP Slow Start phase, where the window grows rapidly and the sender needs to signal credit for potential future congestion before it happens.

The RFC identifies two main sources of inaccuracy. First, without SACK, the sender cannot precisely count lost bytes and must estimate. Second, with classic ECN, the receiver can only signal that at least one congestion mark occurred in the last RTT, not the exact number. Accurate ECN feedback (AccECN), defined separately, helps but is not yet widely deployed. The RFC recommends ConEx implementations use the most accurate feedback available but acknowledges that some inaccuracy is inevitable and acceptable.
sections.eli5: Timing matters: if you mark a packet a second after congestion, the network has already moved on. You have to mark packets in real time. And counting exactly how much congestion happened is hard without detailed feedback from the receiver.
